title: A Review of ARIMA vs. Machine Learning Approaches for Time Series Forecasting in Data Driven Networks
authors: Kontopoulou, V.I.; Panagopoulos, A.D.; Kakkos, I.; Matsopoulos, G.K.
tldr: Reviews comparative studies of ARIMA and machine learning models for time series forecasting across finance, health, weather, utilities, and network traffic, finding AI approaches generally superior but with notable exceptions where ARIMA excels.
problem_and_motivation: The scientific literature lacks a comprehensive summary comparing ARIMA and machine learning time series forecasting methods. A systematic review is needed to establish relative performance and identify conditions favoring each approach. This gap impedes informed model selection for practitioners.
approach: Conducted a selective literature review of studies explicitly comparing ARIMA with machine learning, deep learning, and hybrid models.
Organized reviewed studies by model category (SVM, tree-based, deep learning) and application domain.
Focused on comparative studies published primarily after 2018 to ensure contemporary relevance.
Extracted performance metrics (RMSE, MAPE, MAE, MSE, R²) from each study for cross-comparison.
Identified and analyzed exceptions where ARIMA outperformed machine learning models.
Synthesized findings to characterize dataset and problem conditions favoring each approach.
findings: AI algorithms display better prediction performance than ARIMA in most reviewed applications.
Hybrid statistical-AI models consistently outperform their individual components.
ARIMA outperforms SVM and deep learning models in cases of linear data relationships or limited data ranges.
num: ARIMA had RMSE = 36.18 vs. SVM RMSE = 0.028 for gold price prediction, favoring SVM.
num: Hybrid ARIMA-NARNN achieved RMSE values 35.3% better than ARIMA alone for COVID-19 forecasting.
SARIMA outperformed LSTM and GRU for offshore wind speed forecasting due to seasonal handling.
ARIMA outperforms machine learning for small datasets, short-term forecasts, and linear time dependencies.
Machine learning methods improve relative performance as sample size grows.
Deep learning models (LSTM) require large datasets to train effectively.
LSTM and GRU outperformed ARIMA in non-linear COVID-19 data for most countries, with RMSE values 40 times smaller.
key_figures_tables: Table 2: Summary of ARIMA vs. SVM comparison studies → SVM generally outperforms ARIMA across domains.
Table 3: ARIMA vs. tree-based model comparisons → XGBoost frequently outperforms ARIMA.
Table 4: ARIMA vs. deep learning studies → LSTM typically outperforms ARIMA for large datasets.
Table 5: ARIMA vs. hybrid models → Hybrid approaches consistently beat ARIMA alone.

definitions.definition: Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average, a classical time series model.
Seasonal ARIMA with additional seasonal parameters.
Support Vector Machine, a supervised learning method for classification and regression.
Long Short-Term Memory, a recurrent neural network with memory gates.
Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, an ensemble learning method.
eXtreme Gradient Boosting, an optimized GBDT implementation.
Akaike Information Criterion for model selection, balances fit and complexity.
Bayesian Information Criterion, similar to AIC with higher complexity penalty.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This review provides a comprehensive, multi-domain comparison of ARIMA and machine learning time series forecasting methods. It synthesizes results across finance, health, weather, utilities, and network traffic, identifying conditions favoring each approach. The work establishes that hybrid models consistently outperform individual methods, and identifies data linearity, size, and seasonality as key drivers of model selection. It also highlights the importance of proper benchmarking against classical methods for ML forecasting research.
directly_justifies: Machine learning models outperform ARIMA in most forecasting applications.
Hybrid statistical-AI models steadily outperform their individual parts.
ARIMA is more suitable for small datasets and linear time dependencies.
LSTM and GRU require large datasets to outperform ARIMA effectively.
ARIMA outperforms ML for seasonal univariate data like offshore wind speed.
limits: Primarily reviews comparative studies without performing original empirical analysis.
Focuses on aggregated findings without controlling for study-specific methodological variations.
Does not provide a quantitative meta-analysis of effect sizes across studies.
Limited coverage of tree-based models compared to deep learning and SVM approaches.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: A systematic scan across all 14 topic domains identified three high-relevance areas: predictive modeling algorithms (6.A, 6.B), evaluation frameworks (12.A, 12.B), and forecasting algorithm comparisons (6.A, 6.B, 12.B). Medium relevance was assigned to budget recommendation evaluation (12.C) due to the discussion of forecasting evaluation methodologies. Contextual relevance was assigned to topics related to spending cycles (2.D), expense categorization (3.A), finance system landscapes (4.A, 4.B), and anomaly detection (8.A), as these appear in reviewed applications but are not central to the paper's core contribution. Topics with no relevance include Filipino-specific demographics (1.A-C), culturally specific practices (2.A-C), cold-start problems (5.B-C, 7.E), offline-first design (9.C), privacy (10.A-C), engagement (11.A-B), savings and debt management (13.A-C), and ML deployment (14.A-C), as these are not addressed by the review. The paper's topical coverage centers on comparative algorithm evaluation rather than domain-specific finance system design.

limitations: Selective literature review; may not be exhaustive for all domains. [unacknowledged]
